q1.attribution: —Historian's account of Ibn Khaldun's theory of state formation in the fourteenth-century Islamic world
q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE element of Ibn Khaldun's explanation for the rise of dynasties.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of dynastic decline according to the interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way Ibn Khaldun's theory could be applied to a state outside the Islamic world in the period 1200–1450.

sample_answers.a: Dynasties rise, in his view, on asabiya — the group solidarity built through shared hardship in nomadic or tribal life, which gives a group the cohesion to conquer and rule.
sample_answers.b: He argues that luxury and settled urban life erode the ruling group's solidarity within a few generations, leaving rulers dependent on paid soldiers and crushing taxes, which invites overthrow by a tougher new group.
sample_answers.c: The theory could be applied to the Mongol Empire: united by steppe solidarity under Chinggis Khan, it fragmented within generations as the successor khanates settled into the luxurious courts of China, Persia, and Russia and lost their unifying cohesion.

q1.stimulus: Writing in North Africa in the 1370s, the scholar Ibn Khaldun argued that dynasties rise on the strength of group solidarity — asabiya — forged in the hardships of nomadic life, and then decline as city luxury softens later generations. Rulers who begin as vigorous tribal chiefs become, within a few generations, palace-bound monarchs dependent on mercenaries and heavy taxation, until a new group with fresh solidarity overthrows them. For Ibn Khaldun, this was not a story about one dynasty but a recurring cycle in the history of states.

q2.attribution: —Adapted from Ibn Khaldun, Muqaddimah (Introduction to History), 1377
q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE claim Ibn Khaldun makes about luxury in the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE piece of evidence from the history of Dar al-Islam between 1200 and 1450 that supports his claim.
parts.c: Explain ONE limitation of Ibn Khaldun's cyclical theory as an explanation for state formation.

sample_answers.a: He claims that settled urban luxury weakens a ruling group's solidarity and causes its power to pass to others who still possess the toughness of desert life.
sample_answers.b: The Abbasid caliphate's decline fits his claim: as Baghdad grew wealthy, the caliphs relied on Turkish slave-soldiers rather than Arab tribal solidarity, and real power slipped first to the Buyids and then to the Seljuks.
sample_answers.c: The theory struggles with states that endured for centuries without collapsing on schedule — the Ottoman Empire, for example, maintained power for over 600 years through institutions such as the devshirme and a standing army, not just tribal solidarity.

q2.stimulus: When people settle in cities and grow accustomed to luxury, their group solidarity weakens. The ruling house, once vigorous, becomes accustomed to a life of ease and pleasure, and its power passes to others who still possess the toughness of desert life.

q3.attribution: Copy of the world map of al-Sharif al-Idrisi, drawn 1154 for Roger II of Sicily (1929 copy by Konrad Miller)
q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the map that reflects the geographic knowledge of the Islamic world in the twelfth century.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the advanced state of geographic knowledge shown on the map.
parts.c: Explain ONE way the map illustrates cultural interaction between the Islamic world and Christian Europe.

sample_answers.a: The map shows a detailed, connected Afro-Eurasian world — from the Atlantic coast of Spain and North Africa across to India and China — reflecting knowledge gathered along Muslim trade and pilgrimage routes. (Note: south is at the top of the map.)
sample_answers.b: One cause was the expansion of Islamic trade networks and the hajj pilgrimage, which moved merchants, scholars, and sailors across vast distances, generating firsthand geographic information that court geographers compiled.
sample_answers.c: The map was made by a Muslim scholar working at the court of a Christian Norman king in Sicily, showing direct collaboration and the transfer of Islamic learning into Latin Europe.

q3.stimulus: A copy of the world map drawn by the Muslim geographer al-Sharif al-Idrisi in 1154 for Roger II of Sicily. South is at the top; the map depicts the known world from Spain to China with detailed coastlines of the Mediterranean, Arabia, India, and East Africa.
